items.title: Stateless servers: server ko aapko yaad kyun nahi rakhna chahiye
items.one_idea: A stateless server keeps no per-user memory between requests: the user's state lives in a shared session store (or in a signed token the client sends), so any server behind the load balancer can answer any request, and a dead or added server loses nobody's session.

items.visual_idea: A user and a load balancer in front of three server boxes. First design: the cart icon sits inside Server A only, the next request lands on Server B and its cart is empty, then Server A turns grey (dead) and the cart disappears. Second design: the cart icon moves out into one shared store box (key = session id, value = cart) that all three servers read from; requests now hop between servers and the same cart shows every time, and one server can be removed or added with no loss.
items.everyday_anchor: Adding items to a shopping cart on a shopping app, then a new request lands on a different server and the cart is empty; or a bank clerk who must check your file every time instead of remembering your face.
items.example: EXAMPLE: user adds 2 items to a cart, request 1 goes to Server A, request 2 to Server B. With state inside Server A, request 2 sees an empty cart; with the cart in a shared session store keyed by the session id from the cookie, request 2 sees both items. Item counts are EXAMPLE, not measured. Sticky sessions are shown as the workaround, with the catch that if the sticky server dies its sessions are lost and load can skew (our reasoning, said as 'typically').
facts_to_verify: HTTP is stateless by default; cookies carry a session ID so the server can recognise the same browser (MDN Cookies, fetched)

Stateless protocol: the receiver does not retain session state from previous requests; each request carries the context it needs; advantages include scalability, reliability, visibility (Wikipedia, fetched)

Session persistence (sticky): NGINX Plus adds a session cookie to the first response and sends later requests with it to the same server; ip_hash sends the same client address to the same server unless it is unavailable (NGINX docs, fetched)
Session state can be kept in an external key-value store, user identifier as key and session data as value (Redis page, fetched). A vendor page, so say 'for example Redis', no performance numbers
The AWS sticky-sessions page returned only its title when fetched, so no AWS claim is made; the claim that a sticky server dying loses its sessions is our reasoning, label it so, or drop it
Do not claim JWT or any token detail unless a page is fetched at build time; if used, show it as one line 'client sends a signed token' with a fetched source
No code shown; if a header example is shown, use the MDN Set-Cookie / Cookie example as printed
